JSON: Name: social_worker_cyber_counseling_roles Title: A cluster-randomized controlled evaluation of social worker-led counseling units to improve organizational cybersecurity awareness, reporting, and recovery outcomes Short Hypothesis: Implementing a dedicated social worker-led counseling unit within an organization causes a measurable increase in staff cybersecurity awareness scores and incident reporting rates, and a reduction in phishing susceptibility, compared with organizations that receive standard technical training or no intervention. Related Work: Existing work on cybersecurity practice emphasizes technical controls, awareness campaigns, and formal risk frameworks; separate literature addresses social work responses to technological change, community education, and trauma-informed interventions. Prior cybersecurity awareness studies typically measure training efficacy via simulated phishing and knowledge tests but focus on short-term technical education rather than integrated social support. Social-work literature documents mediation, psychosocial support, and community-level interventions but lacks application in operational cybersecurity settings. Combined studies are limited: proposals and qualitative analyses suggest potential counseling roles (awareness raising, mediation, regulatory advocacy, therapeutic support) but provide small samples, descriptive data, or expert opinion without controlled quantitative evaluation. Limitations in prior approaches include: absence of randomized or matched comparisons, narrow outcome sets centered on knowledge rather than behavioral reporting and resilience, lack of standardized intervention protocols for social workers in cyber contexts, and limited cross-sector generalizability. Abstract: Organizations commonly address cybersecurity through technical controls and short-term awareness campaigns, while the potential counseling role of social workers within cyber incident prevention and response remains under-evaluated. This study proposes and evaluates a structured social worker-led counseling unit deployed in operational organizations to (1) deliver tailored awareness and training, (2) provide psychosocial intervention after security incidents, and (3) mediate between technical teams and affected staff. We will measure behavioral and organizational outcomes—staff awareness, phishing susceptibility, incident reporting rates, and time-to-recovery—using a cluster-randomized controlled design with active and passive controls. The main contribution is an empirically validated intervention model and a multivariate assessment framework linking psychosocial counseling activities to measurable cybersecurity outcomes. Expected outcomes include statistically significant improvements in awareness and reporting and reduced phishing susceptibility in intervention clusters, demonstrating that integrating social work practices into cybersecurity operations yields measurable operational benefits beyond conventional technical training. Experiments: Design: cluster-randomized controlled trial with three arms: (A) social worker-led counseling unit (intervention), (B) active technical training control, (C) passive control (no new intervention). Sample: 60 mid-sized organizations (20 per arm) matched by sector, staff size (100–500 employees), and baseline incident rate; if orgs unavailable, use 90 smaller clusters to preserve power. Duration: 9 months (3-month baseline, 6-month intervention and follow-up). Intervention specification: deploy a standardized unit staffed by two trained social workers per organization delivering (i) monthly group awareness workshops, (ii) individual counseling for incident-affected staff, (iii) liaison sessions with IT/security teams, and (iv) policy-advice meetings. Active control: standardized technical awareness program (monthly workshops, technical phishing simulations) without counseling. Data collection: pre/post staff cybersecurity knowledge test (validated 25-item instrument), monthly simulated phishing campaigns (click-through rate), incident reporting logs (number of reported incidents per 1,000 employees per month), time-to-detection and time-to-containment from incident logs, and staff psychosocial impact measured via the Workplace Stress Scale and a 6-item incident distress questionnaire. Baselines: historical 6-month incident logs and knowledge scores. Evaluation metrics: primary—change in mean knowledge score, change in phishing click rate, change in incident reporting rate; secondary—change in mean time-to-containment, change in psychosocial distress scores. Statistical analysis: intention-to-treat mixed-effects linear models with random intercepts for organization and fixed effects for time and arm; logistic models for phishing click events; difference-in-differences estimators for reporting rates. Power: detect Cohen's d = 0.4 in knowledge score with 80% power at alpha=0.05 requires ~20 clusters per arm with average 50 respondents per cluster. Ablation studies: (1) intervention minus therapeutic component (awareness+liaison only) vs full intervention; (2) staffed by generalist vs cyber-trained social worker; (3) varying intensity (monthly vs biweekly sessions). Sensitivity analyses: adjust for baseline covariates (sector, IT maturity), per-protocol analysis excluding noncompliant clusters, and subgroup analyses by role (IT vs non-IT staff). Risk Factors and Limitations: Potential technical and logistical failure modes: low organizational buy-in leading to incomplete intervention delivery; inconsistent incident log formats and missing data across organizations; contamination between arms (sharing of materials or staff mobility). Data and evaluation biases: self-selection of participating organizations may bias toward more progressive firms; social desirability bias in self-reported awareness and reporting; simulated-phishing habituation effects and learning confounds. Scalability and compute: intervention requires human staffing resources and cannot be scaled by software alone; replication in very large enterprises may need different staffing ratios. Limits to generalization: results may not generalize across sectors with highly regulated incident reporting or to small organizations with limited HR capacity; cultural and legal differences across countries may change acceptability of counseling activities. Measurement limits: incident reporting rate may increase both from improved detection and from increased reporting of minor events, complicating interpretation of security posture; psychosocial metrics may be influenced by external stressors. Ethical and privacy constraints: counseling records and incident details contain sensitive personal data that restrict sharing and may limit external validation. Statistical risks: residual confounding and insufficient cluster-level sample size could reduce power to detect effects.
